scenes.tts: Water holds far less oxygen than air. Yet a trout's gill can bring its blood close to the oxygen partial pressure of the water flowing in. Your lung cannot do that with air. Why not?
scenes.visual: Two panels: a trout gill whose outgoing blood bar nearly matches the incoming water bar, and a lung whose outgoing blood bar is an empty question box.
scenes.narration: Water holds far less oxygen than air. Yet a trout's gill can bring its blood close to the oxygen partial pressure of the water flowing in. Your lung cannot do that with air. Why not?

scenes.tts: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross gills and lungs by diffusion. They move from higher partial pressure to lower. Dry air at sea level is about twenty-one percent oxygen, at a total pressure of about seven hundred sixty millimetres of mercury. So oxygen's partial pressure there is roughly one hundred sixty. The rate rises with area and with the pressure difference, and falls with barrier thickness. So the question is where that difference can be kept up.
scenes.visual: High and low pressure columns across a barrier slab; the air arithmetic chip; Fick's law line with area, pressure difference and thickness highlighted in turn.
scenes.caption: Oxygen and CO2 cross gills and lungs by diffusion. They move from higher partial pressure to lower. Dry air at sea level is about 21% oxygen, at a total pressure of about 760 mmHg. So oxygen's partial pressure there is roughly 160. The rate rises with area and with the pressure difference, and falls with barrier thickness. So the question is where that difference can be kept up.

scenes.tts: In teleost fish, such as trout, each gill carries filaments, and each filament carries thin plates called lamellae. Inside a lamella, blood flows opposite to the water. This is countercurrent exchange. Blood about to leave meets water that has just arrived. So a pressure difference holds along the whole lamella. If both streams ran the same way, they would come close to equal partial pressure partway along. The rest of the lamella would add little.
scenes.visual: Filaments and lamellae named; Water row runs right, blood row runs left, yellow shading shows partial pressure; difference marks all along; then the blood flips to run the same way and the cells after equality are marked as adding nothing.
scenes.narration: In teleost fish, such as trout, each gill carries filaments, and each filament carries thin plates called lamellae. Inside a lamella, blood flows opposite to the water. scenes.tts: Now the mammal lung. In mammals, air flows in and out through the same airways. This is called tidal ventilation. The airways end in tiny dead-ended sacs, the alveoli. Each breath mixes with stale air left behind. Meanwhile blood keeps taking oxygen out of the alveolar gas, and each breath only partly renews that gas. So in an adult human at rest, alveolar oxygen partial pressure is about one hundred millimetres of mercury. Warmed, humidified inhaled air is roughly one hundred fifty. Blood can at best match the alveolar gas.
scenes.visual: A tube with a double-headed arrow ending in a dead-end sac where fresh and stale air mix; then three bars: inhaled 150, alveolar 100, blood at best 100.

scenes.tts: Birds do it differently. Their lungs exchange gas in tubes called parabronchi. Through most of them, air flows the same way during breathing in and breathing out. Capillaries cross the airstream. This is crosscurrent exchange. Each stretch of capillary meets air at a different stage. So mixed blood leaving the lung can hold a higher partial pressure than the air breathed out.
scenes.visual: A tube with two arrows pointing the same way, labelled breathing in and breathing out; capillary bars cross it; a comparison of mixed blood leaving versus air breathed out.

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy two, Johannes Piiper and Peter Scheid compared idealized models of these three arrangements under matched conditions. By their measure, countercurrent moved the most gas. Crosscurrent came next. The mixed pool of a mammal lung moved the least. That ranks arrangements, not animals. Keep this rule: how two streams flow past each other changes gas exchange.
scenes.visual: Three arrangement icons with ranked bars (most, next, least) in idealized models; then a note that it ranks arrangements, not animals.
